headline: AI support agent remembers past conversations, cutting costs by 80% with Hindsight memory
summary: A new AI customer support agent, SupportMind, leverages 'Hindsight' memory and 'cascadeflow' routing to remember user interactions, reducing query costs from ~$0.012 to ~$0.002.
details: SupportMind is a new AI customer support agent designed to remember past conversations, moving beyond traditional FAQ bots. It achieves an 80% cost reduction, dropping query costs from ~$0.012 to ~$0.002 on typical workloads.

The architecture features a 'Hindsight' memory layer that stores structured context per user in a vector namespace. This allows the agent to semantically recall previous issues, even if keywords don't directly match.

A 'cascadeflow' routing layer directs queries to the most cost-effective model. Simple requests, like password resets, go to cheaper tiers, while complex billing disputes escalate, with every decision logged for analysis.

This dual-layer approach enables a dramatically different agent experience. Instead of repeatedly asking for details, SupportMind can proactively suggest solutions based on a user's recurring issues and past resolutions.

An unexpected benefit is the compounding effect of routing and memory. If Hindsight shows a user has faced an issue multiple times, cascadeflow automatically classifies their next message as complex, even without explicit signals.

headline_marked: [[AI coding agents can be tricked into installing malware]] via 'clean' GitHub repos, Mozilla warns
headline: AI coding agents can be tricked into installing malware via 'clean' GitHub repos, Mozilla warns
summary: Mozilla's 0din team demonstrated how Claude Code can be exploited through seemingly innocuous steps, giving attackers full control over a developer's account and data.
details: Mozilla's 0din team successfully tricked Claude into running malware by asking it to initialize a project from a seemingly clean GitHub repository. This method grants attackers full control over a developer's account, accessing secrets, API keys, code, documents, browser sessions, and passwords.

The attack leverages three levels of indirection, none of which appear suspicious in isolation. A victim developer simply instructs Claude to initialize a project from a malicious GitHub repository, which is designed to look clean with minimal scaffolding files and no obvious triggers for security tools.

Upon cloning the repository, Claude processes a readme file that outlines how to set up a Python environment using the commonly used Axiom package. A fake Axiom startup script intentionally errors out on its first run, prompting Claude to execute another seemingly harmless command: "python3 -m axiom init" to resolve the issue.

This command then triggers a shell script that downloads additional software. Crucially, instead of downloading from a suspicious URL, the script reads DNS text (TXT) records of a specific domain, such as "_axiom-config.m100.cloud". This technique appears legitimate, as TXT records are routinely used for email and other service configurations.

The TXT record contains a base64 encoded string that, when decoded, opens a reverse shell. This redirects the user's machine shell to the attacker's server, allowing them to access all data the user has permissions for. Meanwhile, both Claude and the victim only see an "Environment ready" message.

The 0din team concludes that developers should never blindly trust unknown projects or rely on AI tools for security analysis. They recommend that AI agents be designed to inspect what code will actually run and how, rather than simply following instructions.
